profile.title: Bold, Savoury & Adventurous
profile.summary: Your answers point towards red wine, with an interest in richness and savoury flavours. Your choices around a fuller body and a dry finish help shape the suggestions below, rather than fixing you into a single wine personality. Your curiosity about unfamiliar styles leaves space to explore different grapes and ways of making wine. At the table, familiar foods can give you a simple way to notice texture and freshness. This is a starting point based on what you shared, not a measurement of tasting ability. Your preferences can change as you learn.

exercise.title: Notice the weight of a wine
exercise.text: If you choose to taste, compare small samples of a lighter and fuller-bodied wine. Notice how each feels in your mouth, rather than how strong its aroma seems. Write one texture word for each; neither needs to be better. Try a bite of your meal and notice whether the impression changes. Tasting is optional; you can smell, read or spit instead.

exercise.title: Separate fruitiness from sweetness
exercise.text: If you choose to taste, compare small samples of a clearly labelled dry and off-dry wine from the same grape. Smell first, then notice sweetness on the palate and mouth-watering acidity. A fruity aroma does not necessarily mean a wine is sweet. Try a bite of your meal and notice whether the impression changes. Tasting is optional; you can smell, read or spit instead.

exercise.title: Find three words of your own
exercise.text: If you choose to taste, focus on one small sample. Smell it before tasting, then note one aroma, one texture and one impression of freshness. Everyday words are enough. Compare your notes with the label afterwards, rather than searching for a correct answer. Try a bite of your meal and notice whether the impression changes. Tasting is optional; you can smell, read or spit instead.
